主要内容: On March 8, 2018, President Donald Trump signed two proclamations imposing tariffs on steel and aluminum imports, with exemptions for Canada and Mexico. The 25% duty on steel and 10% charge on aluminum were part of Trump's effort to revisit global trade deals, particularly NAFTA. The tariffs, which will take effect in 15 days, were justified by the White House as essential for domestic and economic security. Trump emphasized the importance of a strong steel and aluminum industry for national security, stating, "You don't have steel, you don't have a country." The exemptions for Canada and Mexico are not open-ended and depend on whether changes to NAFTA satisfy Trump. The administration also allows other nations to justify their exclusion from the tariffs if they can demonstrate a satisfactory alternative means for resolving trade inequities. Critics argue the tariffs could worsen global economic relations and trigger a trade war. Financial markets have been volatile since the announcement, and the administration is not expecting significant business backlash despite industries' reliance on cheaper imports. U.S. Steel has announced it is reopening a plant in Illinois, while Century Aluminum officials have indicated that the tariffs could generate 300 new jobs in Kentucky. These developments highlight the potential impact of trade policy on domestic manufacturing and employment.
